claims.text: Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a tensile yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a terminal strain of approximately 13.5%.
A controlled oxygen-interstitial addition is proposed for HfZrTiTa0.53.
Oxygen-doped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi-based alloys provide an analogue for the proposed intervention.
Interstitial oxygen in HfZrTiTa0.53 will form ordered oxygen complexes.
Ordered oxygen complexes will locally impede dislocation motion.
The proposed complexes will promote more uniform strain distribution and enhanced strain hardening under tensile loading.
Oxygen addition will improve the tensile ductility and uniform elongation of HfZrTiTa0.53.
The oxygen-doped HfZrTiTa0.53 will reach approximately 20% uniform tensile elongation, or about a 50% increase over the stated 13.5% baseline.
The oxygen-doped HfZrTiTa0.53 will retain a tensile yield strength near or above 786 MPa.
The oxygen-doped alloy will retain impact-triggered energy release comparable to the baseline alloy.
The hypothesis applies at room temperature under tensile loading at approximately 1×10^-3 s^-1.
The cited oxygen-doped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloy exhibited 1138 MPa yield strength and approximately 20% elongation at room temperature and 1×10^-3 s^-1.
The optimal oxygen concentration and processing conditions for producing ordered oxygen complexes in HfZrTiTa0.53 are not established.
Transfer of the oxygen-induced ductility response from Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi to HfZrTiTa0.53 requires experimental validation.
Baseline and oxygen-doped specimens will be produced with identical melting, casting, and heat-treatment conditions and compared by tensile, compression, and impact tests.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant elongation increase while retaining yield strength within ±5% and comparable impact energy release is specified as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The reported 13.5% value is identified only as terminal strain and is associated with a baseline that also lists compressive strength, but it is subsequently treated as the baseline for uniform tensile elongation. Terminal or compressive failure strain is not interchangeable with uniform tensile elongation.
